questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute how much of a local budget its own revenue covers
questions.stem: A local authority spends 45.0 million in a year, of which 20.0 million comes from its own sources and 25.0 million from transfers made by higher government. What share of its spending does its own revenue cover?

options.text: 28.6 percent, which divides by spending and transfers added, counting the same money twice
options.misconception: puts the transfer into the base as well as into the funding

options.text: 44.4 percent, which is 20.0 divided by 45.0
100.0 percent, which divides own revenue by the spending left after transfers
options.misconception: divides the figure counted by what remains of it, so a fixed sum gives full coverage

options.text: 55.6 percent, which is 25.0 divided by 45.0
options.misconception: reports the share that transfers cover instead of the share own revenue covers

questions.explanation: Coverage means the numerator's share of what the authority actually spends, so the base is the 45.0 of spending and not the total of the two funding streams. Twenty divided by forty-five is 0.4444, which is 44.44 percent. The check is that the two shares of the same base must add to 100: transfers are 25.0 over 45.0, or 55.56 percent, and 44.44 plus 55.56 is exactly 100. The third option adds the transfer to the spending to form a base of 70.0, which counts 25.0 of money twice. The fourth divides by the complement, and 45.0 minus 25.0 is 20.0, so 20.0 over 20.0 gives the full coverage of a sum that is by definition fully self-funded.
questions.hint: Use the authority's total spending as the base, then check that the shares add to 100.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a gap between levels from a gap within a level
questions.stem: Two districts in the same region have per-resident revenue of 900 and 1,500 while every district in the region has per-resident revenue well below the national figure. Which gap does the first comparison describe?

options.text: A gap between districts of the same level, alongside a gap between levels
A gap in a single district, since 900 and 1,500 are revenue figures for one authority
options.misconception: reads two districts' figures as one authority's total and its parts

options.text: A gap in revenue effort, since the higher-earning district is trying harder
options.misconception: converts a difference in capacity into a difference in willingness

options.text: A gap between levels of government, which is what a district comparison measures
options.misconception: describes a district-to-district difference as a level-to-level one

questions.explanation: The two comparisons describe two different gaps and the stem gives both. Districts of the same region are at the same level, so the 900 against 1,500 is a difference between units of the same tier, which is what is meant by a gap within a level. The comparison with the national figure is a different gap again, because it is between a subnational unit and the country as a whole. The second option collapses the two into one and says a district comparison measures a level comparison, which is a category error. The third mistakes two districts for one, and the fourth turns a difference in the amount a district can raise into a claim about its willingness, which the figures cannot establish.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two figures being compared come from the same tier of government.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the two sides of a fiscal assignment
questions.stem: A constitution assigns the collection of a tax to the centre while assigning the spending it funds to districts. What has been assigned where?

options.text: The revenue side to one level and the expenditure side to the other, and they do not match
Neither side, because a split assignment assigns no function to either level
options.misconception: reads a split as an absence of assignment

options.text: Both sides to the centre, since collecting a tax is a national function whatever spends it
options.misconception: ignores the half of the arrangement that is expressly devolved

options.text: Both sides to the same level, since a tax must be collected by whoever spends it
options.misconception: assumes a rule that no constitution has to follow

questions.explanation: Assignment works on two sides and a constitution can treat them separately. The revenue side is the power to raise and collect, and the expenditure side is the power to decide how money is spent; the tax in the stem is on the first and the spending it funds is on the second, so the arrangement is a deliberate mismatch. That mismatch is the usual source of the problem of a level that spends without raising and a level that raises without spending, and it is why many arrangements pair a devolved spending power with a transfer formula. The other three read the arrangement as uniform in a direction it is not. Nothing requires a tax to be collected by whoever spends it, a split is still an assignment of each part, and the spending is expressly not with the centre.
questions.hint: Separate the power to raise money from the power to spend it and ask where each sits.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Assigning a function to a level
questions.learningObjective: apply the criteria for assigning a function to a tier
questions.stem: A function benefits from being decided close to the people affected, and it is also the function with the greatest effect on the country's overall totals. Which consideration should carry more weight in deciding which level takes it?

options.text: Neither is automatically decisive, since the choice is between two defensible values
Deciding close to the people affected, because that is always the better rule
options.misconception: treats one stated value as settled when it is the question in dispute

options.text: The effect on national totals, because only the centre can manage the totals
options.misconception: asserts that only the higher level has the instruments for a national effect

options.text: The effect on national totals, because closeness always produces worse outcomes
options.misconception: asserts an outcome claim about a design question with no support

questions.explanation: The stem sets up a genuine conflict between two reasons for assigning a function, and the honest answer is that neither defeats the other. Deciding close to those affected is a reason for devolution, based on information and on accountability to the people who use the service. The scale of the effect on national totals is a reason for central assignment, based on consistency across the country and on the ability to coordinate. Which dominates depends on how large the effect is and how far the affected people are from the decision, and neither value can be read off the question. The other three settle the conflict by fiat: two of them assert a general superiority for one value, and one goes further and claims an outcome, which is a different kind of claim altogether.
questions.hint: Ask whether either stated reason is a value that the assignment question has to weigh, not settle.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute one region's share of a weighted formula grant
questions.stem: A pool of 500.0 million is shared among three regions using weights of 50 percent for population, 30 percent for the number of residents in poverty and 20 percent for land area, each indicator being taken as the region's share of the national total. Region A has 1,000 thousand residents, 200 thousand of them in poverty, and 40 thousand square kilometres. How much does region A receive?

options.text: 250.00 million, from region A's half share of the national population
options.misconception: uses the population weight alone and ignores the other two indicators

options.text: 166.67 million, from 200 out of 280 thousand poor residents over a third of the pool
options.misconception: applies the poverty weight but gives the largest poor count only a third

options.text: 166.67 million, from an equal third of the pool for each of three regions
options.misconception: divides the pool equally and applies no weight at all

options.text: 238.81 million, from 238.81 out of a 500.0 million pool

questions.explanation: Each indicator has to be converted into a share before the weights are applied. On population, region A has 1,000 of the 2,000 thousand residents, a share of 0.5. On poverty it has 200 of the 280 thousand counted, a share of 0.714286. On area it has 40 of the 600 thousand square kilometres, a share of 0.066667. The weighted score is 0.5 times 0.5, plus 0.3 times 0.714286, plus 0.2 times 0.066667, which is 0.25 plus 0.214286 plus 0.013333, so 0.477619. Applying that to the 500.0 million pool gives 238.8095 million, or 238.81. The scores of the three regions add to exactly 1 and the three grants to exactly 500.0, which is the check that the weights were applied to shares rather than to levels.
questions.hint: Turn each indicator into a share of the national total before multiplying by the weight.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify what a derivation-based grant rewards
questions.stem: A circular states that each region receives a grant equal to the revenue it raised for itself in the previous year, and that a region that raised less will receive less. What does that rule reward?

options.text: The population of each region, since the grant is expressed in per-resident terms
options.misconception: reads a formula on past collections as a formula on residents

options.text: The need in each region, since a poorer region will have raised less and so gets more
options.misconception: reads less collected as more need and reverses the direction of the rule

options.text: The amount a region managed to raise, and penalises a region for raising less
The efficiency of each region's administration, since the grant is paid after the year ends
options.misconception: concludes that a payment rule settles how efficiently money was collected

questions.explanation: A derivation-based grant is a payment for a region's own record, and it works in one direction only. The rule in the circular pays out in proportion to what was raised, so a region that raised more receives more and a region that raised less receives less, and nothing in the formula looks at need, population or cost. The first option states that and is what the sentence says. The second is the exact inverse of the rule, since the regions that raise least are the ones with the weakest tax base, which is not the same as the regions with the most need. The third imports a per-resident basis the formula does not use. The fourth infers efficiency from the timing of a payment, which is a non sequitur: a rule that pays after the fact says when the money arrives, not how well it was collected.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity the formula actually multiplies, and which way it moves.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A block grant and the discretion it carries
questions.learningObjective: identify what a block grant leaves to the recipient

stimulus.body: Extract from a grant schedule, written for this question. Schedule B: (1) The authority receives a single sum for all the services listed in Part 1 and may apply it to any of them. (2) The sum is not varied according to how much the authority spends on any individual service. (3) The authority shall publish an annual statement of the amount received and of the amount applied to each service in Part 1. (4) The schedule does not require the authority to observe any standard of service, and no officer of the central government may inspect the services to which Part 1 applies. (5) If the authority's own-source revenue in a year falls below the level in the preceding year, the sum under this schedule is reduced by the amount of the fall.

questions.stem: A grant schedule pays a single sum that the recipient may apply to any of the listed services, is not varied by what the recipient spends on any one of them, and is cut if the recipient's own-source revenue falls. Which of these features carries discretion?

options.text: The freedom to apply one sum across the listed services without varying it by service
The absence of any standard of service, which allows the recipient to set whatever it likes
options.misconception: converts the absence of a standard into a power to set one

options.text: The reduction when own-source revenue falls, which leaves the recipient free to avoid the cut
options.misconception: describes a sanction as though it were an option open to the recipient

options.text: The requirement to publish a statement, which gives the recipient discretion over what to disclose
options.misconception: turns a reporting duty into a choice about disclosure

questions.explanation: The discretion lies in the pairing of subsections (1) and (2). The recipient is given one sum rather than a sum per service, and is free to apply it across the listed services without the payment being adjusted for what it actually does on any of them, so the choice of how to divide the money sits with the recipient. That is the feature the first option describes. Subsection (3) is a duty to publish, and a duty is not a discretion, which disposes of the second option. Subsection (5) is a mechanical reduction, not an option: a fall in own-source revenue brings the sum down whether or not the recipient regards that as fair. And subsection (4) leaves a gap in the standards rather than conferring a power, so the fourth option mistakes what is missing for something that has been granted.
questions.hint: Find the clause that lets the recipient choose, and rule out the ones that only impose duties.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute a local contribution under a match rule
questions.stem: A central programme offers 60.0 million towards a project, on condition that the local authority contributes 25 percent of the total cost. What is the local authority's contribution, and what is the total cost?

options.text: 80.0 million from the authority, on a total cost of 80.0 million
options.misconception: reports the grossed-up total as if it were the authority's own contribution

options.text: 15.0 million from the authority, on a total cost of 75.0 million
options.misconception: reads the match as a share of the central sum rather than of the total

options.text: 60.0 million from the authority, on a total cost of 80.0 million
options.misconception: reports the central government's three-quarter share as the authority's own

options.text: 20.0 million from the authority, on a total cost of 80.0 million

questions.explanation: The condition is expressed as a share of the total, so the central sum is the remaining three-quarters of that total rather than a part of it. Sixty is 75 percent of the total, so the total is 60 divided by 0.75, which is 80.0, and the authority's 25 percent of 80.0 is 20.0. The way to see the difference between the two readings is to check the ratio: 60 plus 20 is 80, and 20 over 80 is exactly 25 percent, so the pair is consistent; 60 plus 15 is 75, and 15 over 75 is 20 percent, which is not the rate the rule specifies. The second option uses 15, which is 25 percent of 60 rather than of the total, and the third reports the grossed-up total as though it were the authority's share. The fourth option reports 60.0, which is the central government's own three quarters of the 80.0 and not a figure the authority can owe.
questions.hint: Work out the total first, because the match is a share of the total and not of the grant.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: read a transfer schedule and quantify an unfunded function

stimulus.body: Extract from a schedule accompanying a devolution agreement, written for this question. Part 2 lists the functions transferred to the regional authority, and against each is stated the sum the national government will pay for it in the first year. Function 1, road maintenance, is listed at 12.0 million against an estimated cost of 12.0 million. Function 2, adult social care, is listed at 30.0 million against an estimated cost of 41.0 million. Function 3, emergency fire services, is listed at 9.0 million against an estimated cost of 9.5 million. Function 4, waste collection, is listed at 8.0 million against an estimated cost of 8.0 million. The schedule states that the sums are for the first year only and that no sum is payable in respect of any function not listed in Part 2.

questions.stem: A transfer schedule pays 12.0, 30.0, 9.0 and 8.0 million for four functions whose estimated first-year costs are 12.0, 41.0, 9.5 and 8.0 million. What does that show about the transfer as a whole?

options.text: The transfer leaves the authority short on two of the four functions, and adult social care dominates the gap
The transfer leaves the authority short on all four functions by the same amount each
options.misconception: assumes an equal gap where the four gaps differ

options.text: The transfer fully funds every function listed, since each has a sum against its name
options.misconception: ignores the difference between the sum and the estimated cost

options.text: The transfer fully funds every function, so the authority is left with a surplus to allocate freely
options.misconception: turns a shortfall on two functions into a general surplus

questions.explanation: Compare each sum with the cost beside it. Road maintenance receives 12.0 against 12.0 and waste collection 8.0 against 8.0, so both are met in full. Emergency fire services are short by 0.5 and adult social care by 11.0, so two of the four are underfunded. The unpaid total is 11.5, of which 11.0 is the single shortfall on adult social care, which is 95.7 percent of the gap, so that one function dominates it. That is what the first option says. The second and third read the presence of a sum as evidence of adequacy, which the columns make checkable, and the third then compounds the error by turning a shortfall on two functions into a surplus on all of them. The fourth claims a uniform gap that the four pairs of figures do not show.
questions.hint: Take each cost minus the sum beside it and look at the pattern of the four results.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply a debt ceiling to a local authority's accounts

stimulus.body: Extract from a circular issued by a ministry of the interior, written for this question. Circular 7/3, paragraph 3: A local authority shall not take on any new borrowing without the written consent of the Secretary of State where, at the end of the financial year immediately preceding the borrowing, its total outstanding debt exceeds one and a half times the revenue it raised for itself in that year. Paragraph 4: For the purposes of paragraph 3, revenue raised for itself does not include any transfer received from a government at another level, and total outstanding debt does not include borrowing the repayment of which falls on revenue from a designated source. Paragraph 5: The consent required by paragraph 3 is a matter for the Secretary of State's discretion, and is not subject to any requirement to give reasons.

questions.stem: A circular requires written ministerial consent for new borrowing where a council's outstanding debt exceeds one and a half times the revenue it raised for itself, and excludes transfers from the calculation. A council's debt is 96 million and the revenue it raised for itself last year was 52 million. What follows?

options.text: Its ratio is 1.85, above 1.5, so it needs written consent before borrowing more
Its ratio is 1.85, which is below 1.5, so it may borrow without consent
options.misconception: reads a ratio above the threshold as though it were below it

options.text: It may not borrow, because the circular gives the minister a discretion but no power to consent
options.misconception: reads a discretionary power as if the power itself were absent

options.text: Its ratio is 0.55, because the debt should be set against the money it is owed
options.misconception: turns the division round to produce a figure below the threshold

questions.explanation: The ratio is the debt divided by the authority's own-source revenue, which is 96 over 52, and that is 1.8462, so it is 1.85 to two decimal places. The ceiling in paragraph 3 is one and a half, and 1.85 is above it, so the consent requirement is engaged. Two things follow that the stem is designed to test. First, paragraph 4 excludes transfers, so adding a transfer to the 52 would change the calculation and is not permitted. Second, paragraph 5 makes the consent a matter of discretion with no requirement to give reasons, so the council cannot treat a refusal as something to be argued by asking for the reasoning. The second option reads a figure above the threshold as below it, the third inverts the division, and the fourth mistakes discretion for the absence of a power.
questions.hint: Divide the debt by the authority's own revenue and compare the result with the threshold.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify what central approval of local borrowing is for
questions.stem: A national government may approve or refuse a local authority's request to borrow, and a refusal leaves the authority with fewer options than it had before the rule. What is the rule principally for?

options.text: Replacing local lenders, since the centre borrows at a lower rate than any authority
options.misconception: supposes the centre borrows on the authority's behalf at a better price

options.text: Reducing the exposure of something that would otherwise be borne widely
Giving the centre control over which local projects are built in each area
options.misconception: reads a financial approval as a planning veto over projects

options.text: Protecting the centre's own revenue, since local borrowing would otherwise reduce national tax
options.misconception: asserts an effect on national tax that local borrowing does not have

questions.explanation: The rule exists because the cost of a local default is not borne by the locality. A local authority that borrows against its own revenue and cannot repay may stop paying for services or, in the stronger versions, be bailed out by the centre, and in either case the loss spreads beyond the authority's own residents. Approval lets the centre act on that exposure, which is what the first option says. The rule is a financial control, not a planning one, which disposes of the second option: approving a loan says nothing about which projects are built. The third invents an agency relationship, since the centre is not borrowing on the authority's behalf. And the fourth asserts an effect on national tax that the mechanism does not have, because the centre's revenue is not reduced when a locality borrows.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the loss if a local borrower cannot repay.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Soft budget expectations and a bailout
questions.learningObjective: explain how an expected bailout changes a borrower's incentives
questions.stem: A central government has rescued two local authorities that ran out of money, and commentators say the rescues have taught other authorities that they need not restrain themselves. What is the mechanism?

options.text: The rescue reduces the amount other authorities can borrow from the same lenders
options.misconception: asserts a market effect that the mechanism in the argument does not use

options.text: The rescue gives every authority the same limit on its own borrowing as the rescued ones
options.misconception: claims a uniform rule emerges from two discretionary decisions

options.text: The expected rescue lowers the cost to a borrower of taking risks it should not take
The rescue proves that the authorities were reasonable, so their borrowing was sound
options.misconception: converts a change in expected consequences into a vindication of the past

questions.explanation: The mechanism is a change in what a borrower expects to bear. If a rescue is available, the downside of a bad loan is smaller than it looks to the authority taking it, so a decision that would be irrational if the authority bore the full loss becomes rational if the centre absorbs part of it. The authorities that now borrow freely are responding rationally to a changed incentive, which is exactly why the rescues have the effect described. The second option is a separate claim and a different one: it says the rescued authorities were right, which is a judgement about their circumstances and not about anybody else's expectations. The third posits a lender-side mechanism that the argument does not need, and the fourth mistakes two individual decisions for a general rule.
questions.hint: Ask what changes in the calculation a borrowing authority makes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The property-tax base and its valuation
questions.learningObjective: explain why the valuation of a property-tax base governs its yield
questions.stem: Explain why a local authority that relies on a tax on property values collects more or less than it expects when the assessments used to compute the charge are out of date, and say what a revaluation does to the yield.

answer.exemplar: The charge is usually expressed as a rate applied to an assessed value, so the yield is the product of the rate and the assessed base, and the two move independently. A rate set as a number of units per thousand of assessed value therefore does not track the market. Three things can happen. If assessments are stale and understate current values while the rate is left unchanged, the authority collects less than a rate applied to current values would produce, because each property is charged on an old figure. If assessments are stale and overstate current values, it collects more than a current valuation would give, because the base is inflated. This is why reassessment and a rate change are two separate decisions: raising the rate on an understated base partly cancels the reassessment, and lowering the rate can be a way of absorbing a large rise in the base without changing the bill of a typical property. A general revaluation that moves the base upward therefore raises the yield at an unchanged rate, and any change in the yield beyond that has to come from the rate itself. What a revaluation does not do is tell the authority how much money it should raise. That is a budget decision, and the yield is only the arithmetic that connects the two. It is also worth separating the effect on total collections from the effect on an individual household, because a general reassessment can raise the total while leaving most bills roughly unchanged, if the rate is adjusted at the same time.

questions.explanation: A strong answer treats the yield as the product of a rate and a base, works through what stale assessments do to that base in both directions, and then distinguishes the effect on total collections from the effect on an individual bill. Crediting the point that a revaluation and a rate change are separate decisions is what makes the answer clearly better than one that stops at saying the yield rises.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a rate expressed as an amount per thousand of assessed value when the assessments move.

questions.learningObjective: compute the collected yield of a property charge
questions.stem: An authority has 240,000 chargeable properties with an average assessed value of 150,000, and a rate of 12 per thousand of that value. It collects from 78 percent of the properties on the list. What does it collect?

options.text: 403,200,000, from 1,680 a property on the whole of the list
options.misconception: applies the collection rate to the per-property figure instead of the total

options.text: 336,960,000, from 1,800 a property on 78 percent of the list
432,000,000, from 1,800 a property on the whole of the list
options.misconception: ignores the collection rate the stem states

options.text: 95,040,000, from the 22 percent of the list that pays nothing
options.misconception: calculates the loss instead of the collection

The second option reports the gross figure. The third reports the uncollected amount, which is 95,040,000 and is the complement. The fourth applies 78 percent to the per-property charge of 1,800, producing 1,404, and then charges that to the whole list rather than to the 78 percent that pays.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Local insolvency and the order of priority
questions.learningObjective: read an insolvency clause and state what priority it sets

stimulus.body: Extract from a statute on the financial administration of local authorities, written for this question. Section 9: (1) Where an authority is unable to meet a liability out of the money available to it, it shall apply that money first to the payment of wages and salaries, then to the payment of sums due to the government for the purposes of tax, then to the payment of sums due to suppliers of goods and services, and only after that to any other liability. (2) The order set by subsection (1) does not affect the order in which any two of the payments within the first three places are to be made. (3) An authority that is unable to meet a liability within subsection (1) shall notify the supervising ministry within fourteen days. (4) Failure to comply with subsection (1) is a ground on which the supervising ministry may make an order in respect of the authority, and subsection (3) is not a condition of the making of such an order.

questions.stem: A statute orders an authority short of money to pay wages, then tax owed to the government, then suppliers, then everything else, and says the order does not fix the sequence within the first three places. Which of these does the statute actually establish?

options.text: A power for the ministry to order payments, which the authority may disregard until notified
options.misconception: reads the ministry's power as dependent on the authority's notification

options.text: A ranking of four classes of payment, with the sequence inside the first three left open
A complete sequence, in which wages precede tax and tax precedes suppliers
options.misconception: converts a ranking with an open sequence into an exact order of payment

options.text: A duty to notify the ministry, which must be met before any payment at all is made
options.misconception: turns a notification duty into a precondition for lawful payment

questions.explanation: What the statute fixes is the ranking, and subsection (2) is explicit that the ranking is not a full sequence. It places wages above tax above suppliers above everything else, and then declines to order the three within the first three places, so a statement about the statute has to be a statement about a ranking. The second option asserts an exact sequence that the text declines to give, and the first pair in the ranking is not thereby a guaranteed order. Subsection (3) is a duty to notify within fourteen days, not a condition on making the payments, which disposes of the third option. And subsection (4) is the opposite of the fourth option's reading: it makes failure to comply a ground for an order, and it says expressly that notification is not a condition of the order being made.
questions.hint: Separate what is ordered from what is left to be settled locally.

questions.topic: A county in a unitary state
questions.learningObjective: identify what a county is within a unitary system
questions.stem: A unitary state has a single legislature and no constitutionally guaranteed regional governments, and one of its administrative areas is a county whose council runs services locally. What is that county?

options.text: A component of a federation, since it runs services with its own revenue
options.misconception: concludes federal status from local service delivery alone

options.text: A second chamber of the legislature, since its members represent part of the country
options.misconception: confuses an elected council with a national legislative chamber

options.text: A sovereign unit whose powers cannot be altered by the national legislature
options.misconception: claims entrenchment that a unitary constitution does not grant

options.text: An administrative subdivision created by the centre, not a constitutionally entrenched unit of government

questions.explanation: In a unitary state the constitution establishes one level of constitutional authority, and any subnational bodies exist because the centre created them and could reorganise them. A county that runs local services is real and may have its own revenue, but its standing is administrative and delegated, which is what the first option says. The second option mistakes the presence of local functions and local money for federal status, and federal status turns on where constitutional authority is located rather than on what a body does. The third option asserts the entrenchment that is the defining feature of a constituent unit of a federation and is precisely what a unitary constitution withholds. The fourth confuses a local council with a chamber of the national legislature, which is a different body with a different electorate and a different reach.
questions.hint: Ask where the constitutional authority sits, not what the body does.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute the administrative cost of a duplicated function

stimulus.body: Extract from an audit of local administration, written for this question. The audit examined three functions administered by both the national government and the districts. For each function it records the cost of administration at district level, taken as 0.8 million per district, and the cost of the corresponding administration at national level. Road inspection: 4 districts at district level, 0.8 million each, giving 3.2 million; national administration 0.8 million. Food safety inspection: 4 districts at district level, 0.8 million each, giving 3.2 million; national administration 0.8 million. Building regulation: 4 districts at district level, 0.8 million each, giving 3.2 million; national administration 0.8 million. The audit records that in each of the three cases the national administration duplicates work the districts already perform, and it makes no finding that either level is unnecessary.

questions.stem: An audit finds three functions administered at both levels, with district administration costing 0.8 million per district across four districts, so 3.2 million per function, and national administration costing 0.8 million for the same function. What does the audit support?

options.text: That 2.4 million is duplicated, and that neither level is therefore necessary at all
options.misconception: turns a finding of duplication into a finding that a whole tier is redundant

options.text: That 2.4 million is duplicated within a total of 12.0 million, of which 9.6 million is district administration
That 9.6 million of district administration is unnecessary, since the centre already does the work
options.misconception: inverts which of the two levels is treated as the duplicate

options.text: That all 12.0 million of administration is unnecessary, since the districts already do the work
options.misconception: converts duplication at one level into uselessness at both

questions.explanation: The arithmetic is fixed by the extract. Three functions at 3.2 million each is 9.6 million of district administration, and three national administrations at 0.8 million each is 2.4 million. The 2.4 million is the part the audit records as duplicated work, and the 9.6 million is the district cost that the extract nowhere questions, so the first option states the pair correctly. The second option reaches the right figure for the duplication and then adds the two together as if 12.0 were the district figure, which it is not. The third option treats duplication as total waste, and the extract is explicit that no finding is made that either level is unnecessary. The fourth reverses the roles of the two levels, which is the classic error in reading a duplication finding: the question is which level is doing the same work twice, not which level is redundant.
questions.hint: Separate the cost at each level before deciding which part is the duplicate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Layering and the cost of overlap
questions.learningObjective: distinguish layering from duplication
questions.stem: In one arrangement a district carries out work on behalf of a region, so two tiers handle one task; in another, a district and a region each assess a similar matter independently. How do the two differ?

options.text: The first is two functions at two tiers, the second is one function over two tiers
options.misconception: swaps which arrangement is the single function and which the pair

options.text: The first is one function spread over two tiers, the second is two functions at two tiers
Both are layering, since two tiers are involved in each case in some way at all
options.misconception: treats the presence of two tiers as settling the question

options.text: Both are duplication, since a function is performed more than once in each arrangement
options.misconception: assumes repetition of the same function where one case delegates it

questions.explanation: The two arrangements differ in what is being repeated. Where a district performs work on behalf of a region there is one function and one set of outputs, delivered through two tiers, which is what layering means: a single task stacked on top of another. Where a district and a region each assess a similar matter on their own there are two functions, each with its own decision and its own output, and the fact that they overlap in subject matter is what makes that duplication. Both involve two tiers, so the third option's test settles nothing. The fourth option mistakes delegation for repetition: a delegated function is carried out once, by the tier to which the delegation was made.
questions.hint: Count the functions, not the tiers involved in each case.

options.misconception: confuses a representative body with an administrative one

options.text: To give local authorities a collective voice where each is too weak to be heard alone

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a guarantee of self-government from a power of supervision
questions.stem: A constitution guarantees local self-government and separately provides that the national government may supervise the exercise of local powers. How do the two provisions relate?

options.text: They pull against each other, and the balance between them sets how autonomous the local level is
Supervision overrides the guarantee wherever the two conflict, so autonomy depends on goodwill
options.misconception: asserts a priority the constitution nowhere establishes

options.text: The guarantee is void wherever supervision is exercised, so supervision has no effect
options.misconception: treats a constitutional guarantee as excluding an expressly provided power

options.text: They say the same thing, since supervision is a form of self-government
options.misconception: identifies a limit on a power with the power itself

questions.explanation: The two provisions are two ends of the same scale, and a constitution that contains both has not resolved the question of autonomy. A guarantee of self-government is a claim about the local level's own sphere, and a power of supervision is a claim about the centre's interest in how that sphere is used; where both appear, the amount of local autonomy is set by how far supervision can reach, and a court may be asked which provision prevails in a case where a supervisor has gone further than the guarantee allows. That makes the first option right, and it explains why such constitutions are usually read as containing a principle rather than a formula. The second option collapses a limit into the power it limits. The third and fourth each pick a winner the text does not name, and the second of them makes autonomy depend on the centre's disposition, which is a very different arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask how much room is left for local discretion once supervision is available.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: read an equalisation table and compare shares against need

stimulus.body: Extract from an equalisation formula, written for this question. A pool of 400.0 million is divided among three regions in proportion to the difference between the standard cost of providing a standard set of services to each resident and the revenue each region can raise for itself. The standard cost is 1,200 per resident. Region A: 250,000 residents; revenue raised for itself 20.0 million; standard cost 300.0 million; difference 280.0 million. Region B: 1,000,000 residents; revenue raised for itself 130.0 million; standard cost 1,200.0 million; difference 1,070.0 million. Region C: 400,000 residents; revenue raised for itself 60.0 million; standard cost 480.0 million; difference 420.0 million. The formula states that the three differences are the whole basis of division and that no other factor is to be taken into account.

questions.stem: A pool of 400.0 million is divided among three regions in proportion to the gap between the standard cost of services and the revenue each can raise for itself. The gaps are 280.0, 1,070.0 and 420.0 million. What does that produce, and how does it compare with population?

options.text: Grants of 63.3, 241.8 and 94.9 million, and region B's grant share is above its population share
options.misconception: gets the amounts right and then reverses the direction of the comparison

options.text: Grants of 38.1, 247.6 and 114.3 million, which is the basis of what each region raises itself
options.misconception: substitutes the region's own revenue for the gap the formula specifies

options.text: Grants of 63.3, 241.8 and 94.9 million, and region B's grant share is just below its population share
Grants of 60.6, 242.4 and 97.0 million, which is the population basis the formula excludes
options.misconception: divides the pool by residents and ignores the gaps the formula names

questions.explanation: The basis is the gap, and the three gaps total 280.0 plus 1,070.0 plus 420.0, which is 1,770.0. Region A therefore takes 280 over 1,770 of the pool, which is 0.158192, or 63.3 of the 400.0. Region B takes 1,070 over 1,770, which is 0.604520, or 241.8, and region C takes 420 over 1,770, which is 0.237288, or 94.9. The three add to exactly 400.0, which is the check that the basis was used rather than one of the alternatives. Against population, region B holds 1,000,000 of 1,650,000 residents, which is 60.61 percent, while its grant share is 60.45 percent, so its grant share is 0.15 of a point below its population share. That is the comparison the formula is designed to produce, and it is what the first option states. The second divides by residents, the third by the revenue each region raises, and the fourth has the amounts right and the comparison the wrong way round.
questions.hint: Divide each gap by the total of the three gaps, then compare the largest region's share with its residents.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: assess the strongest objection to derivation-based equalisation
questions.stem: A government defends its equalisation formula on the ground that a region should be paid in proportion to what it collects for itself, since that keeps the payment simple and the region in control of its own revenue. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: It is too complicated for regional treasurers to apply without national guidance
options.misconception: turns a defence of simplicity into a defence of simplicity

options.text: It tends to give least to the regions with the weakest tax base, which is where need is greatest
It cannot be applied at all, because regions have no revenue of their own to count
options.misconception: denies the very revenue base the payment formula is built on

options.text: It gives a region too little control, since the payment is fixed by a national formula
options.misconception: objects to a lack of local control that the formula actually provides

questions.explanation: The objection is that the measure tracks ability rather than need. Regions differ in how much they can raise because their tax bases differ, and a region with a weak base will both collect less and have more need, so a formula that pays in proportion to collections moves money away from the places with the greatest shortfall. That is a real distributive criticism, and it is the one the formula has to answer. The second option restates the defence rather than answering it, and simplicity is not a distribution. The third reverses the relationship, since a national formula limits local discretion over the payment without limiting it over revenue. And the fourth contradicts the premise of the payment, which is that regions do collect revenue of their own.
questions.hint: Ask what a region that raises little looks like on this formula.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain what a reserved power guarantees to a lower level
questions.stem: A constitution lists a set of matters that only a region may legislate on, and says the centre may legislate on all other matters. What does the reservation do?

options.text: It makes the region's powers exclusive in practice as well as in law
options.misconception: equates a legal floor with an outcome, which depends on capacity

options.text: It prevents the centre from regulating the reserved matters at all, on any ground
options.misconception: converts exclusivity into an immunity from any central involvement

options.text: It fixes a floor of exclusive authority the centre cannot take over by ordinary legislation
It allows the centre to legislate on the reserved matters whenever no region has done so
options.misconception: invents an unused-power route that a reservation denies

questions.explanation: A reservation is a statement about the location of legislative authority, and its function is to set a floor. It means that the matters named cannot be taken over by the centre through ordinary legislation, which is what makes the arrangement different from one where the centre holds a general power and shares it. The first option says that. The second option invents a route the text does not provide: the centre's power extends to the other matters, not to a reserved matter that a region has left unused, since leaving a power unexercised does not transfer it. The third adds an outcome claim, since whether a region can in practice use a power reserved to it depends on its capacity and not on the reservation. And the fourth reads exclusivity as a bar on any central involvement at all, which is much stronger than what reserving a legislative power means.
questions.hint: Ask what the centre cannot do without a constitutional change.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain what a residual clause allocates
questions.stem: A constitution assigns certain powers expressly to the centre and certain powers expressly to the regions, and adds that any power not so assigned belongs to the centre. What is the effect of that last clause?

options.text: A new power belongs to both levels at once, and each may act within its own field
options.misconception: assumes a concurrent power where the clause allocates exclusively

options.text: Every new power belongs to the regions, since the clause only names what is not assigned
options.misconception: reads an express assignment to the centre as if the clause were silent

options.text: The centre holds every new power unless the constitution is changed to move it
A new power belongs to whichever level first exercises it in practice
options.misconception: invents a rule of first use that the clause does not state

questions.explanation: A residual clause answers a question the express assignments cannot, which is what happens to a matter nobody thought about. It allocates everything the constitution has not allocated, and the choice of level is a choice about the default. Where the default is the centre, as here, a new subject falls to the centre unless the constitution is amended, so the position of the region is secure only in respect of what the text has given it and depends on amendment for anything else. The second option reads the clause as if it were silent about the default. The third invents a rule of first exercise, which some arrangements have but not this one. The fourth treats an exclusive allocation as a concurrent one, which would leave the same matter with two legislatures at once.
questions.hint: Ask where a matter the constitution never mentions would go.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: read a constitutional guarantee and state what it protects

stimulus.body: Extract from a constitution, written for this question. Article 30: (1) The existence of elected local authorities and their right to manage their own affairs is guaranteed. (2) Any alteration of the boundaries of a local authority, and any transfer of a function from a local authority to another body, shall require the consent of the local authority concerned. (3) The national government may give directions to a local authority on the exercise of a function conferred on it by statute, and a local authority shall comply with any such direction. (4) A local authority shall be entitled to such funds as are necessary for the discharge of its functions, and the basis on which those funds are computed shall be set out in the law.

questions.stem: A constitution guarantees elected local authorities and their management of their own affairs, requires their consent to a change of boundary or a transfer of function, allows the centre to give binding directions, and provides that local authorities are entitled to the funds their functions require. What does the article establish?

options.text: A local authority free of any binding direction from the centre, which the article forbids
options.misconception: reads the permission to direct as a prohibition on directing

options.text: A protected local sphere, with supervision and funding that are both allowed
A purely nominal protection, since the centre may direct and fund on its own terms
options.misconception: treats supervision and funding as though they removed the guarantee

options.text: A guarantee of financial independence, since the funds are described as necessary
options.misconception: turns an entitlement to funds into control of the whole budget

questions.explanation: The four subsections do different work and the article is built around that division. Subsections (1) and (2) protect the local sphere: authorities are to exist, to manage their own affairs, and to be consulted before their territory or their functions are taken away, which is a real limit on the centre. Subsection (3) then permits binding directions, and it is a permission rather than a prohibition, so the second option is wrong about the direction. Subsection (4) guarantees funds without specifying the basis in the article itself, so the third option's claim of pure nominality does not follow, because a constitutional entitlement is not the same as nothing. And the fourth option converts an entitlement to sufficient funds into control of the entire budget, which the wording does not support.
questions.hint: Sort the four subsections into what they protect and what they permit.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A central power over a failing municipality
questions.learningObjective: read an intervention clause and state what it permits

stimulus.body: Extract from a statute on municipal administration, written for this question. Section 6: (1) Where a supervisory commission has reported that a municipality is unable to discharge the duties imposed on it by law, the national government may by order appoint a commissioner to carry out those duties in place of the municipal council. (2) An order under subsection (1) shall specify the matters in which the commissioner acts in place of the council, and may be limited to a period not exceeding two years. (3) While a commissioner is so acting, the municipal council and its elected members shall be suspended from the functions specified in the order. (4) The powers of a commissioner under this section are those stated in the order, and no others. (5) Nothing in this section affects the power of a court to examine whether an order under this section has been lawfully made.

questions.stem: A statute lets the national government appoint a commissioner to act for a municipal council where a commission has reported the council unable to discharge its duties, with the order limited to specified matters and to two years, the council suspended in those matters, the commissioner given no other powers, and the courts left to examine the order. What does the section permit?

options.text: A permanent transfer of the functions to the commissioner, since no end date is fixed
options.misconception: converts a time limit of two years into a permanent arrangement

options.text: A limited, defined and reviewable displacement of an elected council for a fixed period
The exercise by the commissioner of whatever powers the municipality exercises
options.misconception: denies the limit that subsection (4) places on the commissioner's authority

options.text: The removal of the council, since suspension of its functions is in issue
options.misconception: converts a specified suspension into a removal of the authority itself

questions.explanation: Every feature of the section points the same way, and together they say what kind of power this is. Subsection (1) supplies a threshold, since a commissioner may be appointed only on a report that the council cannot discharge its duties. Subsection (2) limits the order in subject matter and in time, to two years at most. Subsection (3) suspends the council only in the matters specified, which is why the second option overstates it into a removal. Subsection (4) confines the commissioner to the powers the order states, so the third option's wider grant is excluded by the text. Subsection (5) leaves the order open to a court, which is what makes the arrangement reviewable and, with everything else, what the first option says it is: bounded on five sides at once.
questions.hint: Check each subsection for a limit rather than a grant.

questions.learningObjective: identify what asymmetric devolution means and costs
questions.stem: One region in a system of local government has its own written constitution and its own source of revenue, while the other regions have neither. What follows from that difference?

options.text: The arrangement is unlawful, because devolution must be uniform across every unit
options.misconception: asserts a uniformity requirement that asymmetry does not breach

options.text: The units are not constitutionally equivalent, so the arrangement has to be justified on its own terms
The special region is no longer part of the same state, since its status now differs

options.text: The other regions are not governments at all, since only a constitution makes a government
options.misconception: denies the standing of units that plainly exercise local functions

questions.learningObjective: identify the practical problem of a concurrent power
questions.stem: A constitution gives both the centre and the regions power to regulate building safety, and two levels have since made different rules on the same question in the same area. What is the characteristic difficulty that follows?

The rules can conflict, and the only solution is for the centre to withdraw from the subject
options.misconception: prescribes withdrawal as though it were the sole remedy

options.text: There is no difficulty, because the stricter rule simply applies wherever both apply
options.misconception: assumes a rule of stricter-is-better that the text does not contain

options.text: There is a difficulty only where the levels are elected, and none where they are appointed
options.misconception: restricts the problem to one form of local authority

questions.explanation: A concurrent power means two bodies can make rules about the same activity in the same place, and it creates the problem of which applies. Where a person must comply with a local rule and a national rule that impose different requirements, the ordinary expectation that there is one answer has failed, and resolving it may require a court or a rule about priority that the constitution has not supplied. That is the first option. The second option offers a remedy as though it were a consequence, and the whole reason concurrency is sometimes accepted is that a withdrawal would be a loss of power. The third assumes that the stricter rule prevails, which is a plausible design choice but not a consequence of concurrency and not always workable where the rules are alternatives rather than additions. And the fourth invents a restriction: the problem arises from overlapping authority, not from how the local body was chosen.

The first option says that. The second option confuses a ruling about entitlement with the exercise of the function, which remains where the ruling puts it. The third overreaches: a ruling determines the case before the court, and turning it into a general rule for other regions needs either a provision to that effect or a different reasoning. questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: read a set of accounts and describe the balance behind them

stimulus.body: Extract from a region of a unitary state's published accounts, written for this question. Total revenue for the year: 62.0 million. Revenue from the region's own sources: 17.4 million. Revenue from the national government: 44.6 million. Total expenditure: 71.0 million. The published standard cost of providing the set of services the region is responsible for is 1,050 per resident, and the region's resident population is 68,000. The national equalisation pool for the three regions that share this standard is 400.0 million, and the difference between the standard cost and own-source revenue for the three regions is 96.0, 180.0 and 124.0 million respectively. The accounts state that the standard cost is a reference figure for comparison and is not a sum the region is entitled to receive.

questions.stem: A region's accounts show revenue of 62.0 million, of which 17.4 million is its own and 44.6 million is transferred, against expenditure of 71.0 million, with a standard cost of 1,050 per resident and 68,000 residents. Which reading is sound?

options.text: Own revenue covers 24.5 percent of spending, and the region is 9.4 million short of its standard cost
Own revenue covers 24.5 percent of spending, and the region is 9.0 million short of its standard cost
options.misconception: confuses the shortfall against the accounts with the shortfall against the standard

options.text: Own revenue covers 28.1 percent of revenue, and the region is fully funded to its standard cost
options.misconception: uses own revenue as a share of the whole and denies a shortfall the standard reveals

options.text: Own revenue covers 71.9 percent of revenue, and the region is short of its standard cost by 71.4 million
options.misconception: reports the transfer share and treats the whole standard cost as a shortfall

questions.explanation: The two figures have different bases and both can be checked. Own revenue against spending is 17.4 over 71.0, which is 24.51 percent. The standard cost is 68,000 residents at 1,050 each, which is 71.4 million, and the region's total revenue of 62.0 million falls 9.4 million short of that. The first option states both. The second takes 9.0, which is the gap between expenditure and revenue in the accounts, and mistakes an overspend for a shortfall against the standard; the two are close but they are not the same quantity. The third divides own revenue by total revenue, which is 28.06 percent and answers a different question, and then denies the shortfall. The fourth reports the transfer's share of revenue as though it were own revenue's, and treats the entire standard cost as though none of it were already funded.
questions.hint: Check which base each percentage uses, and separate the accounts gap from the standard-cost gap.

options.misconception: treats lobbying as a function of headcount alone

options.text: It will succeed, because a region cannot be refused without breaking the system of local government
options.misconception: assumes a veto over the centre that a region does not hold

options.text: It may succeed where the region's case can be made in terms the centre also values

questions.topic: Fragmented provision across a metropolitan area
questions.learningObjective: compute the cost of separate provision against a pooled one
questions.stem: A conurbation of 2.1 million residents is served by six separate authorities that each collect the same material. Each separate authority costs 1.4 million a year in fixed cost plus 0.42 million for every 100,000 residents it serves. If the six pooled the service under one authority with a fixed cost of 1.4 million and the same rate, what would pooling save?

options.text: 0.00 million a year, since the cost per resident is unchanged by pooling
options.misconception: assumes a pooled service costs the same as a separate one

options.text: 8.40 million a year, from removing the six fixed costs entirely
options.misconception: subtracts all six fixed costs and keeps the pooled fixed cost as well

options.text: 1.40 million a year, from removing the fixed cost of one authority
options.misconception: counts the removal of a single fixed cost instead of five

options.text: 7.00 million a year, from replacing six fixed costs with one

questions.explanation: Only the fixed costs differ, because the variable rate is stated to be the same under either arrangement. Under separate provision the fixed element is six times 1.4, which is 8.4, and the variable element is 0.42 for each 100,000 of 2.1 million residents, which is 0.882, so the total is 9.282. Under pooling the fixed element is 1.4 and the variable element is the same 0.882, so the total is 2.282. The difference is 7.000, and the check is that 8.4 minus 1.4 is 7.0, so pooling removes five of the six fixed costs and leaves one. That is what the first option says. The second subtracts the whole 8.4 as though the pooled arrangement had no fixed cost, and the third is refuted by the fact that the two totals differ. The fourth counts only one removal.
questions.hint: Compare the fixed elements, since the rate per resident is the same in both arrangements.

questions.learningObjective: explain what pooling changes and what it does not

Which authority is responsible for the service, which ceases to have any duty in the matter

options.misconception: reduces the number of duty-holders to one when all still hold a duty

options.text: The standard the service must meet, which the receiving authority may set for itself
options.misconception: concedes a standards power the arrangement does not create

questions.learningObjective: identify how a rate cut can cost a unit revenue
questions.stem: Two neighbouring units set the same charge on a given activity. One then cuts its rate by 10 percent, and over the following year the volume of the activity in that unit rises by 30 percent while the other unit's volume and revenue are unchanged. What follows about the unit that cut?

options.text: Its revenue is 20 percent higher, because a rise of 30 and a fall of 10 leave a gain of 20
options.misconception: adds the two percentage changes instead of multiplying the factors

options.text: Its revenue is 17 percent higher, from 1.3 times the volume at 0.9 times the rate
Its revenue is unchanged, because a 30 percent volume rise and a 10 percent rate fall cancel
options.misconception: treats the two percentage changes as offsetting one another

options.text: Its revenue is lower, because a fall in the rate must reduce revenue whatever happens to volume
options.misconception: assumes a rate cut always reduces revenue, ignoring the change in volume

questions.explanation: Revenue is the rate multiplied by the volume, so the two changes have to be multiplied rather than added. Take the original revenue as 100 units on a base of 1,000. After a 10 percent cut the rate is 0.9 of what it was, and after a 30 percent rise the base is 1.3 of what it was, so the new revenue is 0.9 times 1.3 of the old, which is 1.17, or 17 percent more. The second option is the arithmetic error: 1.3 and 0.9 do not cancel, because losing a tenth of the price is not the same as the volume rising by a third. The third option states a rule that holds only when the volume is unchanged, which the stem says it is not. The fourth adds the percentages to get 20, when the two movements are a change in a price and a change in a quantity and only multiply. The break-even here would be a volume rise of 1 over 0.9, which is 11.11 percent, so a rise of 30 percent is comfortably past it.

options.misconception: ignores that the cost is borne while the benefit is not paid for

options.text: It gives the unit a reason to charge the neighbours, which is a remedy the arrangement denies
options.misconception: invents a charge the arrangement has no provision for

options.text: It gives the unit a reason to provide less of the service than its own residents would justify
It gives the unit a reason to provide more, since residents beyond its border are also helped
options.misconception: reverses the effect by crediting the beneficiaries outside the unit

options.misconception: accepts a proxy measure as if it measured the objective

options.text: A good average achieved by declining complaints, while the underlying number unresolved rises
A fall in the number of complaints, since residents stop raising them
options.misconception: infers a change in resident behaviour the arrangement does not affect

options.text: No effect, because managers are free to disregard a target they cannot meet
options.misconception: assumes a target can be disregarded without consequence

questions.learningObjective: identify what a fiscal zone does
questions.stem: A region sets lower tax rates than its neighbours inside a designated industrial area, and the arrangement is described as a fiscal zone. What does it do?

It shifts tax revenue to the centre, since only the centre may vary a rate
options.misconception: asserts a rule about rate variation the arrangement contradicts

options.text: It equalises the region's rate with the national average rate, whatever the neighbours do
options.misconception: confuses a zone rate with an average rate

options.text: It increases the region's revenue, since a lower rate is paid on a larger volume of activity
options.misconception: assumes a bigger volume is guaranteed by the lower rate

The third option asserts a rule the arrangement contradicts, because a zone cannot exist if only the centre may vary a rate. The fourth confuses a negotiated rate with an average of anything.

questions.topic: The cost of an investment incentive
questions.learningObjective: put a subsidy's cost per job against what it buys

stimulus.body: Extract from a regional development agreement, written for this question. The region agrees to pay a firm a subsidy of 4.0 million over five years, on condition that the firm establishes a plant employing 250 people in the region. Three further firms receive the same subsidy on the same terms, so the region's total commitment is 12.0 million. The region's resident workforce is 9,000. options.misconception: reports one firm's subsidy as though it were the region's total

options.text: 12.0 million for 750 jobs, and the region will also recover part of the sum in tax
options.misconception: invents a tax return that the agreement says the region does not receive

options.text: 12.0 million for 750 jobs, and 750 jobs is 8.3 percent of the resident workforce
12.0 million for 750 jobs, and the region paid about 1,333 for every worker in the workforce
options.misconception: divides the subsidy by the whole workforce and calls that the cost of the deal

Ten years earlier the same authority recorded Progressive Alliance 14 seats, Civic Union 19, District Independents 7, and a turnout of 40 percent. The declaration states that the Civic Union contests only this and two other district elections, that the Progressive Alliance contests all forty authorities in the region, and that a seat is filled by the candidates receiving the most votes, whether or not they stand under a party label.

options.misconception: reads an overall turnout figure as a figure for one party's supporters

questions.topic: An executive appointed by the council
questions.learningObjective: identify the defining feature of a council-appointed executive
questions.stem: In one form of local leadership a council appoints a manager to run the administration, and the manager reports to the council rather than to the residents. options.misconception: denies a combination that is the arrangement's normal setting

That is a real constraint on the claim, and it is what the first option says. The second confuses insecurity of the post with effectiveness, which may be the opposite relationship since a secure manager can plan further ahead. The third invents an electoral requirement the arrangement does not have, and the fourth denies a combination that is the ordinary setting for it.
questions.hint: Ask to whom the manager is accountable when the two disagree.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A local executive answerable to the council
questions.learningObjective: read a charter clause and state what it establishes

stimulus.body: Extract from a local government charter, written for this question. Clause 9: (1) The council shall appoint a clerk and may by notice remove the clerk. (2) The clerk shall be responsible for the administration of the authority's functions, and shall give the council such advice as the council requires. (3) The clerk may be required by the council to attend any meeting of the council and to answer questions, and the council may by resolution express no confidence in the clerk. (4) A vote of no confidence does not of itself remove the clerk from office. (5) Nothing in this clause authorises the council to issue a direction as to the manner in which an officer exercises a discretion conferred on the officer by law.

questions.stem: A charter lets the council appoint and remove its clerk, requires the clerk to run the administration and advise the council, requires attendance at meetings and questions, allows a vote of no confidence, and states that such a vote does not itself remove the clerk and that the council may not direct the exercise of a discretion conferred by law. What does the clause establish?

options.text: An officer who need not attend the council, since the clause makes attendance optional
options.misconception: converts a duty to attend into an option not to attend

options.text: A council that may direct the officer in the exercise of a discretion conferred by law
options.misconception: takes the clause's final sentence for the opposite of what it says

options.text: Removal and the expression of no confidence, with the officer's own legal discretion left intact
Removal only, since a vote of no confidence is expressly without legal effect
options.misconception: reads a provision with stated effect as having none

questions.explanation: The clause distinguishes three things that are easily run together. Subsection (1) is the power of removal, which is what makes the office answerable. Subsection (3) adds a political tool, the vote of no confidence, and subsection (4) says in terms that the vote is not itself a removal, which is a real difference and not an empty one: the vote records a political judgment, and the removal is a separate act. Subsection (5) then protects something different again, namely a discretion conferred on the officer by law, which the council may not direct. So the clause establishes removal and the expression of no confidence while leaving the officer's legal discretion alone, which is the first option. The second overstates the effect of subsection (4). The third inverts subsection (5), which is a prohibition and not a grant. The fourth turns a duty in subsection (3) into an option.
questions.hint: Separate the political instrument from the legal power, and read the last subsection for what it forbids.

questions.learningObjective: work out a recall threshold against a stated turnout
questions.stem: A charter allows the removal of a local executive if a recall petition bearing the signatures of 10 percent of the persons who voted at the preceding local election is filed. The authority has 500,000 registered electors and 35 percent of them voted at that election, so 175,000 votes were cast. How many signatures are needed?

options.text: 17,500, which is a tenth of the 175,000 who voted at the last local election
20,000, which is a tenth of the 200,000 who would vote at 40 percent turnout
options.misconception: applies the tenth to a turnout the charter does not point to

options.text: 175,000, which is the whole of the vote cast at the last local election
options.misconception: treats the turnout itself as the threshold the charter specifies

options.text: 50,000, which is a tenth of the 500,000 whose names are on the roll
options.misconception: uses the electoral roll as the base the charter does not name

questions.explanation: The charter names the base, and the base is the persons who voted at the preceding local election. Thirty-five percent of 500,000 is 175,000 votes cast, and a tenth of that is 17,500 signatures, which is what the first option reports and the check that the figure is a tenth of 175,000 rather than of anything else. The second option applies the tenth to the roll of 500,000, giving 50,000, which would be the answer under a differently drafted rule. The third applies it to a turnout of 40 percent, which is the turnout recorded at an earlier election and is not the one the charter points to; at that turnout the vote would have been 200,000 and a tenth of it 20,000, which is the figure the third option reports and the wrong base for this purpose. The fourth option mistakes the turnout for the threshold.
questions.hint: Apply the tenth to the persons the charter names, not to the roll.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the difficulty of a two-level policing arrangement
questions.stem: In a system where national officers police serious crime and regional officers police everything else, on whose instructions do regional officers act on an investigation that a national officer has begun?

options.text: The official of whichever level has the larger budget for the year
options.misconception: makes command a function of resources rather than of law

options.text: The arrangement has to settle that question, and the rules may leave a gap between the two chains
The national officer, since a national function outranks a regional one at every point
options.misconception: supplies a general priority rule that such arrangements do not contain

options.text: The regional officer, since the regional force is closer to the events in question
options.misconception: adopts proximity as a rule of command in a chain of authority

questions.explanation: Splitting a function between two chains of command creates questions about coordination that the arrangement has to answer, and the question in the stem is one of them. A serious-crime investigation that begins nationally may need regional officers to act, and the rules have to say who directs them, whether the regional officer reports to the regional chain while doing national work, and what happens if the two chains give different instructions. Where the rules do not cover a case, there is a gap, which is what the first option says. The other three all assert a general priority that such arrangements do not contain. A national function is not automatically superior at every point, proximity is not a rule of command, and budget size is not a source of authority.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rules say who directs a regional officer doing national work.

questions.topic: A school system run at regional level
questions.learningObjective: identify what regional control of schools changes
questions.stem: A region rather than individual authorities controls the recruitment of teachers, the curriculum framework and the allocation of staff between its districts. What does that arrangement make possible that district control does not?

options.text: Moving a teacher between districts to equalise provision across the region
Offering a local wage supplement wherever a district chooses to raise one
options.misconception: describes a further centralisation rather than an effect of it

options.text: Employing staff who are answerable to a district council and to a region at once
options.misconception: asserts a dual accountability that regional employment removes

options.text: Closing a school in one district by a decision taken in another
options.misconception: reads regional control as if it were the loss of any local influence

questions.explanation: Control of recruitment and of staff allocation at regional level is what makes it possible to treat the region's provision as a single problem rather than as forty separate ones. A manager who can move a teacher has a tool for closing a gap in one district by drawing on another, and that is the first option. The second is the opposite direction, since a regional employer sets the pay and a district supplement is a local decision that regional control would remove rather than enable. The third takes the arrangement to imply that local influence has been eliminated, when the more accurate description is that the decisions move up a level. The fourth invents a dual accountability, which regional employment dissolves rather than creates.
questions.hint: Ask what a regional manager can do with staff that no district manager can.
