questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Devolution of a service and its ongoing cost
questions.learningObjective: read a transfer clause and work out the continuing liability

stimulus.body: Extract from a devolution agreement, written for this question. Clause 3: The function of issuing premises licences shall be transferred to the regional authority with effect from 1 April, and the regional authority shall be responsible for the service from that date. Clause 5: The national government shall pay the regional authority a one-off grant equal to 60 percent of the estimated first-year cost of the function, that cost being estimated at 24.0 million. Clause 7: The regional authority shall provide the service in accordance with the standard set by national regulation, and no variation of that standard may be made without national consent. Clause 9: The grant payable under clause 5 is a one-off payment and no payment is payable in respect of any later year. Clause 11: Where the national government makes a request in writing, the regional authority shall provide the national government with such information as the request specifies.

questions.stem: An agreement transfers a licensing function to a region, pays a one-off grant of 60 percent of an estimated first-year cost of 24.0 million, requires the national standard with no variation without consent, and provides for no payment in later years. What does the agreement leave with the region?

options.text: A continuing duty to run the service at the national standard, and 9.6 million of the first-year cost
A duty to run the service only until the grant is spent, after which the function returns
options.misconception: invents a reversion the agreement nowhere provides

options.text: A continuing duty, but with no power to vary the standard without national consent being needed
options.misconception: misreads the consent requirement as though it were unnecessary

options.text: A continuing duty to run the service, and 14.4 million of the first-year cost
options.misconception: reports the grant as the amount the region still has to find

questions.explanation: Clause 3 puts the region in charge of the service from the transfer date and clause 9 ends the financial support after the first year, so the duty and the cost sit with the region thereafter. The arithmetic gives the region's own share of the first year: 60 percent of 24.0 million is 14.4, so the remaining 40 percent is 9.6, and that is the figure the first option gives and the second option mistakes for the grant. Clause 7 makes the standard a national one, so the region's discretion over the service is bounded, and clause 9's silence about later years means the whole of the later cost is the region's. The third option invents a reversion that would need a clause and is not there, and the fourth option is a double negative that ends up denying a requirement the clause clearly imposes.
questions.hint: Take the grant as a share of the first-year cost and then read what the agreement says about later years.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Land use and the local plan
questions.learningObjective: identify what a local plan does and does not settle
questions.stem: An authority must prepare a plan setting out how land in its area is to be used, and individual planning decisions must be consistent with it. What does the plan settle, and what does it leave open?

options.text: It settles the general pattern of uses, and leaves each individual decision to be taken on its facts
It settles nothing, because every decision has to be taken afresh by the authority
options.misconception: denies the consistency requirement the plan imposes

options.text: It settles the general pattern and every individual decision, so no discretion remains anywhere
options.misconception: removes the discretion that a plan is required to leave

options.text: It settles each individual application as it is made, and leaves the general pattern open
options.misconception: reverses which of the two functions the plan performs

questions.explanation: A plan is a statement of intended uses for an area, and its effect on an individual application is a requirement of consistency rather than a decision. The plan therefore fixes the general pattern, in which a given piece of land is for housing or for industry or for open land, and leaves the particular application to be assessed on its own facts against that pattern. The first option says that. The second reverses the two functions, and a plan that decided each application as it came would leave nothing to plan. The third is contradicted by the requirement of consistency, and the fourth removes the discretion that a plan is supposed to leave, since the whole point of setting a pattern is to leave room for judgment about particular cases within it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the plan decides an application or the area the application sits in.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Discretion in deciding a planning application
questions.learningObjective: identify what constrains the exercise of planning discretion
questions.stem: A planning officer may refuse a permission, and the authority's members may overturn that decision, provided they give reasons and the reasons are good. What does this arrangement do to the discretion?

options.text: It transfers the discretion to the members, since the officer's view is only provisional
options.misconception: replaces the officer's power with the members' and calls that a transfer

options.text: It leaves the discretion in place and makes the exercise of it open to challenge on its reasons
It removes the discretion, since an officer's decision may be replaced by a political one
options.misconception: turns a check on reasons into the removal of the power to decide

options.text: It leaves the discretion untouched, since the reasons do not affect the decision
options.misconception: assumes reasons are required but irrelevant to the outcome

questions.explanation: The arrangement separates the power to decide from the adequacy of the reasons, and it is the reasons that are open to challenge. A member who overturns an officer has to be able to say why, and if the reasons cannot be found good the decision does not stand. So the discretion is not removed, which disposes of the second option, and it is not merely formal, which disposes of the third: a required reason that could never fail to be good would be no check at all. The fourth option misreads the relationship, since the officer's power is not provisional in the sense of belonging to somebody else, and the power to determine an application remains with the authority. The reason-giving requirement is a check on how the power is used, not a relocation of it.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be shown if a decision is challenged, not who makes it.

questions.topic: A preventive rule on local debt
questions.learningObjective: apply a preventive debt rule to a set of accounts
questions.stem: A rule requires a local authority to keep its total debt at or below two and a half times the revenue it raised for itself in the preceding year. One authority's debt is 480 million and its own-source revenue was 120 million. What follows, and by how much?

options.text: It is above the rule, and it must reduce debt or raise revenue by 72.0 million to comply
options.misconception: gives the rise in revenue needed and calls it the adjustment needed

options.text: It is above the rule, and it must reduce debt or raise revenue by 300.0 million to comply
options.misconception: reports the debt permitted at the cap as the amount of the excess

options.text: It is above the rule, and it must reduce debt or raise revenue by 180.0 million to comply
It is below the rule, since four times revenue is inside a limit of two and a half times spending
options.misconception: misremembers the limit and substitutes spending for revenue

questions.explanation: The ratio is the debt divided by own-source revenue, which is 480 over 120, exactly 4.0, and the limit is 2.5, so the authority is above the rule. The debt permitted at the cap is 2.5 times 120, which is 300, and the excess is 480 minus 300, so 180.0. That is the first option. The second option reports a real figure with the wrong label: 72.0 is the rise in own-source revenue that would bring the ratio down to 2.5, since 480 over 2.5 is 192 and 192 minus 120 is 72, which is a different remedy from the one the question asks about. The third option is above the rule, not below, and the figure it compares against is not the rule's. The fourth option states the permitted debt as the excess.
questions.hint: Work out the ratio first, then the debt permitted at the cap, and take the difference.

questions.learningObjective: search the feasible allocations for the highest number at a cap
questions.stem: Eighty posts are to be allocated among nine offices. Every office must receive at least four posts and no office may receive more than eighteen. What is the largest number of offices that can be given the full eighteen?

options.text: Five, which uses 90 posts and leaves nothing for the remaining four offices
options.misconception: asks for more posts than the total of 80 allows

options.text: Three, which uses 54 posts and leaves 26 for the other six offices
Three, which uses 60 posts and leaves 20 for the other six offices
options.misconception: multiplies three by a cap of 20 rather than by the stated cap of 18

options.text: Four, which uses 72 posts and leaves 8 for the other five offices
options.misconception: gives the five remaining offices less than the four-post floor

questions.explanation: The binding constraint is the floor on the offices that do not get the full eighteen. Four offices at eighteen would take 72 posts, leaving 8 for the remaining five offices, and five offices at a floor of four need 20, so four at the cap is not feasible. Three offices at eighteen take 54, leaving 26 for six offices, and six offices at a floor of four need 24, so 26 is available and an allocation such as 18, 18, 18, 6, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4 satisfies both bounds and sums to 80. An exhaustive search over all the integer allocations that respect the floor and the cap confirms that three is the highest number of offices that can sit at the cap, and three is therefore the answer. The second option fails on the floor, the third has the right count with the wrong arithmetic, and the fourth asks for more posts than exist.
questions.hint: Ask how many posts the offices not at the cap need before you can count the caps.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the transfer of a function actually moves
questions.learningObjective: explain what a transfer of a function does and does not transfer
questions.stem: Explain what a government achieves when it transfers a function to a region, and say why the transfer is rarely complete on the day it is announced.

answer.exemplar: A transfer moves the authority to decide a function from one level to another, and with it comes three things that are often confused. First, decision rights: who takes the decision, who is accountable for it and who a dissatisfied person appeals to. Second, the resources that follow the decision, and third, the capacity to exercise it, which is a separate matter again. The reason the transfer is not complete on the day of announcement is that capacity does not move by declaration. The receiving body needs staff with the relevant skills, who are usually recruited or redeployed rather than transferred whole, so there is a period in which the function has been given but the people to run it do not yet exist in the right place. It needs the systems that hold the records, the budgets, the contractual authority, the data-sharing arrangements, and the legal instructions, each of which has to be established rather than assumed. It needs the standing to give directions to bodies below it, since a function delegated downwards cannot be exercised by a body that has no authority over the body that still holds the relevant premises or systems. And the standard has to be settled, because transferring a function without transferring the means of meeting a standard simply relocates the risk of failure. So the pattern is usually that the decision rights move immediately and visibly, the resources move in the following budget, and the capacity moves over a period measured in recruitment cycles and the transfer of records, which is why a transfer announced in one year is rarely operating as intended in the next. A model answer should identify the three things that move, and should explain the capacity gap as a matter of sequence rather than as a failure of will.

questions.explanation: A strong answer separates decision rights, resources and capacity, and then makes the timing point from the capacity gap rather than from anything about the announcement. Crediting the point that a function cannot be exercised without authority over the bodies that hold the premises and the records is what distinguishes a good answer from one that treats a transfer as a change of a line on an organisation chart.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be in place before an office can run a service it has not run before.

questions.topic: Order of bringing a function into operation
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps in implementing a transfer
questions.stem: A region is to take over a service from a national department on a fixed date. Put these four steps in the order in which they must fall.

options.text: The region's staff take over the work and the service begins to be delivered
options.misconception: delivering the service before the arrangements and the staffing are in place

options.text: Staff are recruited or redeployed and the systems holding the records are established
options.misconception: supplying the service before anyone is in a position to run it

options.text: The region's officers learn how the service is currently run and where it stands
options.misconception: learning how the service works after it has passed to the region

options.text: The legal and financial arrangements for the transfer are settled
options.misconception: settling the arrangements after the service has begun to be delivered

questions.explanation: The sequence runs from entitlement to knowledge to capacity to operation. The arrangements come first, because until the region has the legal authority and the money there is nothing for it to exercise. It then has to learn how the service actually works, which is a step that is often skipped and that cannot be skipped: a service has accumulated practices, records and informal knowledge, and an incoming body that does not acquire them will not be able to keep the service running at the level it was. Staffing and systems follow, because capacity has to exist before it is used, and the operation itself comes last. Reversing any of these produces a gap in the service, and the date of transfer is fixed, which is precisely why the preparation has to precede it.
questions.hint: Begin with what the region must be entitled to do, and end with the step that depends on all of the others.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Local autonomy and its fiscal price
questions.learningObjective: assess the strongest objection to a grant of local autonomy
questions.stem: A government proposes to give local authorities wide discretion over their own budgets, so that decisions are taken close to the people who bear them. A critic says this produces wide differences in service quality between one authority and the next. What is the strongest reply?

options.text: Differences in quality are unimportant, because no resident can compare the services
options.misconception: denies that residents can compare, which is what makes the difference matter

options.text: A common decision is the only way to secure uniformity, so the objection defeats itself
options.misconception: concedes the premise that uniformity requires one decision-maker

options.text: A uniform outcome can be pursued through a common standard rather than a common decision
A common standard would in fact produce the differences the critic fears
options.misconception: claims the remedy would cause the thing it is meant to cure

questions.explanation: The reply separates the requirement of an even outcome from the requirement of a single decision-maker. Discretion about spending is a way of deciding, and it is one source of variation, but the outcome can also be constrained by a standard laid down at the centre, so that every authority is required to meet the same threshold even though each decides for itself how to get there. That is the first option, and it is why a system can combine local discretion with a floor on service quality. The second option accepts the critic's premise that only one decision-maker can produce uniformity, which is exactly what has to be denied. The third declares the differences unimportant on a ground the objection contradicts, since a resident who can compare is the reason the differences matter. The fourth claims the remedy would produce the disease, which is not an argument at all.
questions.hint: Ask how a required outcome could be secured without requiring one decision.
